description: ONE AGENT, ON ONE TASK, UNDER ONE NAMED ACCOUNT. The child of «put-the-crew-to-work», and useful on its own. WHAT TO LOOK AT HERE. (1) THE ASSIGNMENT IS THE ROOT STEP'S INPUT, which is what makes this a child a list can be run over: `for_each` puts each element in the place of the root step's own input, so the same file works launched by hand — fill «the_assignment» in the inputs — and launched once per crew member. (2) THE ACCOUNT VARIES AND THE ENGINE DOES NOT, and that is measured rather than chosen: with the engine read from an input, `sailor flow check` answers «tools no descriptor declares» and the cap falls from a guaranteed one to a stop threshold — it could hold back the next call but never the overshoot of one already running, because nothing can be priced before the run starts. A named engine keeps the cap a cap, and it is `claude-code` because that is the one whose descriptor declares a `native_spend_cap`: with `codex` the same file checks out as a stop threshold instead. Its account variable is `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, which is what `crates/profiles/command-lines.default.json` declares for it. To put another command line to work, name it and its own home variable in a copy of this file. (3) THE ACCOUNT IS A HOME, AND IT IS NAMED, NEVER GUESSED. A home written wrong does not fall back to the default one — the check refuses an empty value before a token is spent, because a variable set to the value the command line would have used anyway disauthenticates it, and every engine that reads it goes from signed in to signed out without saying so. (4) NOTHING IS REFRESHED. Sailor reads the credentials that home already holds and never renews them: a refresh out of band breaks the command line's own access. An account that is not signed in is a refusal to carry back, not a thing to repair here. (5) THE AGENT GETS A TREE OF ITS OWN. A crew works at once, and two agents in one checkout write over each other. (6) THE WALL AND THE CEILING ARE IN THE FILE, not in the good intentions of whoever launches it: `max_spend_micros` is what makes the cap a guaranteed one, and a step that declares none can be admitted and then overshoot inside a single call.

the_assignment.task: say in one line what this tree is for, and stop

with.command:
set -eu
# **AN EMPTY HOME IS NOT THE DEFAULT HOME.** A variable set to the value the
# command line would have used anyway disauthenticates it, so an assignment
# naming no account is refused here, before a token is spent.
[ -n "${ACCOUNT_HOME:-}" ] || { echo 'the assignment names no account home' >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ACCOUNT_HOME" ] || { echo "the account home $ACCOUNT_HOME is not a directory on this machine" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -n "${TASK:-}" ] || { echo 'the assignment names no task' >&2; exit 1; }
printf '%s' "$TASK" | python3 -c '
import json,sys
print(json.dumps({"task": sys.stdin.read(), "home": __import__("os").environ["ACCOUNT_HOME"]}))
'
